questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Solution count of a linear equation
questions.learningObjective: count the solutions of an equation that reduces to an identity
questions.stem: A linear equation in one variable reads 4 times the quantity x minus 2, set equal to 4x minus 8. How many solutions does this equation have?

options.text: Infinitely many, because the equation is true for every real value of x
Exactly one, because cancelling the x terms still leaves a single value
options.misconception: believes cancelling matching terms produces a number to solve for

options.text: None at all, because the two sides are the same with no variable left
options.misconception: reads a true statement for every input as a contradiction

options.text: Exactly two, because an equation that folds back must cross twice
options.misconception: treats an identity as though it had two separate crossing points

questions.explanation: Distributing the 4 on the left gives 4x minus 8, which is exactly the right side, so the equation says something true no matter what x is put in it. That leaves every real number as a solution, and an equation that holds identically is the simplest case of infinitely many. Cancelling the x terms removes the variable and with it the last chance of an equation to be solved, so nothing is left to pin down one value.
questions.hint: Carry out the multiplication and see what is left on each side.

options.misconception: believes any equation that looks solvable must have a solution

options.text: It holds for every x, since both sides rise at the same rate of 7
options.misconception: reads equal coefficients as though they made the two sides equal

options.text: It is empty, since a coefficient of 7 in front of x forces the sides together
options.misconception: believes a matching non-zero coefficient settles the equation

Matching coefficients produce an identity only when the remaining constants match as well, and here they do not. Rearranging cannot rescue the equation, because the rearrangement preserves what is true at each step rather than creating new solutions.
questions.hint: Cancel the x terms and read what statement is left over.

They are perpendicular, since the intercepts differ by the amount of the slope
options.misconception: derives perpendicularity from a gap between intercepts rather than slopes

options.text: They meet once, since different intercepts always force a single crossing
options.misconception: believes differing intercepts guarantee an intersection point

options.misconception: reads a geometric property off the notation instead of the slope

options.misconception: reverses the sign without also taking the reciprocal

options.misconception: copies the slope across and performs no transformation

The reciprocal of zero is the special case of a vertical line, which is why no horizontal answer can appear here.

options.misconception: ties the undefined slope to where a line sits rather than which way it runs

The origin has nothing to do with it: a vertical line anywhere has this property, and its equation simply has no y term to rearrange.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: No solution against infinitely many solutions
questions.learningObjective: explain the difference between an impossible system and one that is always true
questions.stem: Explain the difference between a system of linear equations with no solution and a system with infinitely many solutions, and say what the graphs look like in each case.

answer.exemplar: Both outcomes come from what happens when the two equations are combined, and the graphs show the same thing in a picture. When there is no solution, the two lines are parallel and distinct, so they never cross, and the same fact shows up in the algebra: eliminating one variable leaves a statement of the form 0 equals a number that is not 0, which cannot be true for any values at all. Take 2x plus 3y equal to 12 together with 4x plus 6y equal to 13, where doubling the first equation would give 4x plus 6y equal to 24, not 13, so the two lines share a direction but not a position. When there are infinitely many solutions, the second equation is a multiple of the first, the two graphs are the same single line, and every point on it satisfies both equations; eliminating then leaves 0 equal to 0, which removes a condition instead of adding an impossible one. The test in both cases is the same: simplify until one variable is gone, then read the leftover statement honestly.

questions.explanation: A system's solution set is the set of points common to both graphs, so a parallel pair has an empty intersection while a coincident pair has infinitely many points on the one line they share. The algebra reads the same story, because eliminating a variable either leaves an impossible statement or leaves no statement at all. The distinguishing question is never how many equations there are, but whether the second is a multiple of the first.
questions.hint: Ask what the two graphs have in common, and what the elimination step leaves behind.

Substitute that value back into either original equation for the other
Rewrite or scale the equations so the coefficients of one variable match

Once the variable is gone a single equation remains, and that is what supplies the first value. The back-substitution then supplies the second, and skipping it leaves an answer that satisfies only one of the two equations, which is the usual way an elimination answer turns out to be wrong.
questions.hint: The coefficients must match before anything can cancel.

Multipliers commute only when the same figures are multiplied, and here the two orders act on different intermediate amounts, which is exactly why the results differ. questions.stem: Two points on a line are given as the pair where x is 1 and y is 2, and the pair where x is 4 and y is 11. What is the y-value of the line when x equals 7? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The slope across the two points is 9 over 3, which is 3, so three more units of x add three times 3, which is 9, to the y-value of 11, giving 20. Building the whole rule confirms it: substituting the first point into y equal to 3x plus b gives 2 equal to 3 plus b, so b is negative 1, and 3 times 7 minus 1 is 20. Reading the y-value off the nearest known point instead of continuing the pattern gives 11, which is the usual error.
questions.hint: Work out how much y changes for each unit of x, then move three units along.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: apply a constant of proportionality found from one known pair
questions.stem: A courier charges in proportion to the mass carried, and a 8 kilogram consignment costs 56 dollars. How much does a 13 kilogram consignment cost under the same rate? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The constant of proportionality is the dollars per kilogram, and 56 divided by 8 is 7, so 13 kilograms costs 13 times 7, which is 91 dollars. The check runs the other way: 91 divided by 13 is 7, the same rate as before, which is the test a proportional relationship must pass. Scaling from 8 to 13 by 1.625 and applying that to 56 gives the same 91, and forgetting to scale the cost as well as the mass is the usual slip.
questions.hint: Find the dollars per kilogram from the known pair, then multiply it by 13.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: use a fixed product to find a new output
questions.stem: A quantity y varies inversely with x, and y equals 6 when x equals 4. What is the value of y when x equals 10? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The constant product is fixed at 4 times 6, which is 24, and it has to stay 24 when the input becomes 10, so y is 24 divided by 10, which is 2.4. The check is to return to the original pair, since 4 times 2.4 is 9.6 and not 24, so the sanity test is on the constant and not on one single point. Treating the relationship as direct, and scaling 6 up by the same factor that took 4 to 10, would give 15, which is the mistake that makes a product rule behave like a rate rule.
questions.hint: Find the constant from the known pair, then divide it by the new input.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Intercept read from a standard form equation
questions.learningObjective: find the y-intercept of a line given in standard form
questions.stem: A budget line is given by the equation 2x plus 3y equals 18, where x and y are numbers of two different items. What is the y-intercept of the line this equation describes? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The y-intercept is the output when the input is 0, so substituting 0 for x leaves 3y equal to 18 and y equal to 6. The rearranged rule gives the same figure, since isolating y yields y equal to negative two thirds of x plus 6, and the constant on the right is the intercept. Reading the constant on the wrong side of the equation, or taking 18 as the intercept because it is the number on the right, are the two slips that give 18 instead.
questions.hint: Set the first variable to 0 and solve the equation that is left.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: apply a discount and then a rise with the correct base each time
questions.stem: A ticket priced at 150 dollars is reduced by 40 percent, and the reduced price is then increased by 10 percent. What is the final price in dollars? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The reduction is 40 percent of 150, which is 60, leaving 90, and the increase is 10 percent of that 90, which is 9, so the final price is 99 dollars. Taking the increase on the original 150 instead would add 15 and give 105, which is the base error this item is aimed at. The two percentages also do not cancel, since a 40 percent fall followed by a 10 percent rise leaves the price well below where it started.
questions.hint: Take the reduction from 150, then take the rise from what is left.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: convert a repeating increase into a rate per unit time
questions.stem: Snow settles on a roof at a steady rate, rising 2.5 centimetres every 4 minutes. What is the rate of rise in centimetres per minute? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The rate is the rise over the time, so 2.5 divided by 4 is 0.625 centimetres each minute, and the same figure appears if the whole ratio is written in larger units as 25 millimetres over 240 seconds, which is the same 0.625. Putting the minutes on top would give the time taken per centimetre, which is 1.6 and answers a different question. A steady rate like this is exactly what makes the relationship proportional, since each equal interval adds an equal amount.
questions.hint: Divide the height gained by the minutes it took to gain it.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: solve a system by substitution and confirm it by elimination
questions.stem: A system is 2x plus 3y equals 16, together with y equals x plus 2. What is the value of y? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Replacing y with x plus 2 gives 2x plus 3x plus 6 equal to 16, so 5x equal to 10 and x is 2, and then y is 2 plus 2, which is 4. Elimination agrees: the second equation rewritten as x minus y equals negative 2, tripled to give 3x minus 3y equal to negative 6 and added to the first, leaves 5x equal to 10 again. Both equations then check, since 2 times 2 plus 3 times 4 is 4 plus 12, which is 16, and 4 is indeed 2 plus 2.
questions.hint: Replace y by the rule given, then confirm with a second method.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Using a linear rule beyond the data
questions.learningObjective: apply a fitted linear rule for a year beyond the recorded range
questions.stem: A club had 45 members in 2020 and gained 6 members every year after that, and a student uses the rule y equal to 45 plus 6x, where x counts years since 2020. What does the rule give for 2027? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The year 2027 is 7 years after 2020, so x is 7 and the rule gives 45 plus 42, which is 87 members. Counting the gains one at a time reaches the same place: 51 after one year, 57 after two, and so on up to 87 after seven, which is a good check because it never needs the rule at all. The assumption being made is that the gain of 6 a year continues, since nothing in three or four observations can guarantee what happens years later.
questions.hint: Count the years since 2020 first, then use that as the input.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: choose the scaling that makes two coefficients cancel
questions.stem: In the system 4x plus 3y equals 18 and 5x minus 6y equals 12, which single preparation makes the y terms cancel?

options.text: Multiply the first equation by 2 and add it to the second
Multiply the first equation by 3 and add it, cancelling the 3 against 6
options.misconception: multiplies by a factor that leaves 9 and 6 rather than matching them

options.text: Multiply the second equation by 2 and add it, turning its 6 into 12
options.misconception: scales the equation that already holds the coefficient needed

options.text: Add the two equations as they stand, combining the 3 and the 6 into 9
options.misconception: believes coefficients of different sizes vanish when added

questions.explanation: The y coefficients are 3 and negative 6, so the 3 has to be made into a 6 first, and multiplying the whole first equation by 2 does that, giving 8x plus 6y equal to 36, which added to the second cancels the y terms and leaves 13x equal to 48. Multiplying by 3 would make the coefficient 9, which the 6 cannot cancel, and scaling the second equation leaves the 3 unmatched. Each factor multiplies every term of its equation, which is why the constant on the right has to be doubled along with the coefficient.
questions.hint: Make the smaller y coefficient into the larger one, then combine the equations.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: spot a system in which a common coefficient cancels on subtraction
questions.stem: In the system 5x minus 2y equals 9 and 5x minus 6y equals 3, which operation removes a variable straight away?

options.text: Subtract the second equation from the first, since the 5x terms match
Add the two equations as they stand, matching the 5x terms there
options.misconception: believes two like terms vanish when they are added together

options.text: Multiply the first equation by 6 and then add it to the second
options.misconception: scales needlessly and then chooses the wrong way to combine

options.text: Add 2y to both sides of the first equation to make the terms alike
options.misconception: alters one equation instead of combining the pair

questions.explanation: Both equations carry exactly 5x, so subtracting the second from the first removes those terms and leaves 4y equal to 6, a single equation in a single unknown. Adding the two would instead give 10x minus 8y equal to 12, which still carries both variables, because like terms add rather than cancel. Matching coefficients and choosing subtraction are two separate decisions, and the second follows from the signs once the first is settled.
questions.hint: Compare the coefficients of each variable, then check which way round the subtraction makes them vanish.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: A value that fails the system
questions.learningObjective: correct a reported pair in which the second value was never solved for
questions.stem: A student solves the system x plus y equals 10 and x minus y equals 4 by adding the equations to get 2x equal to 14 and x equal to 7, then reports the answer as x equal to 7 and y equal to 7. What has gone wrong?

options.text: The value of y must come from an equation, and 10 minus 7 gives 3
The value of y must be negative 7, since adding the equations fixed the sign
options.misconception: carries a sign through an addition that cannot create one

options.text: The value of y is 11, from adding the two right sides as well as the x values
options.misconception: adds the constants of both equations together with the unknowns

options.text: The value of y is 14, which is twice the x value that was just found
options.misconception: takes twice the solved value as the second unknown

questions.explanation: Elimination removes one unknown at a time, so after finding x the second unknown still has to be recovered from one of the original equations, and 10 minus 7 is 3. Reporting 7 for y simply repeats the value already found, which is why the pair must be checked: 7 plus 7 is 14, not 10, and 7 minus 7 is 0, not 4, so the reported answer satisfies neither equation. The check is quick and it is the only way to catch a value that was assumed rather than solved for.
questions.hint: The two unknowns are different quantities, so solve the second one from an equation.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain the test that decides whether two quantities vary proportionally
questions.stem: Explain how to decide from a table of values whether one quantity varies proportionally with the other, and describe what the table must look like for the answer to be yes.

answer.exemplar: Proportionality means the output divided by the input is the same number in every row, so the test is to divide and check for a constant rather than to subtract and check for a constant difference. A table of masses of 1, 2, 3 and 4 kilograms beside costs of 4, 8, 12 and 16 dollars gives ratios of 4, 4, 4 and 4, so the constant of proportionality is 4 dollars per kilogram and the relationship is proportional. A table of 1, 2 and 3 beside 4, 9 and 15 fails, because those ratios are 4, 4.5 and 5 and are drifting upwards rather than holding still. The same table also shows why a constant difference is not enough: adding a 3 dollar joining fee to each cost keeps the difference between neighbouring rows equal while destroying the constant ratio, so a relationship can look linear on a graph and still not be proportional. On a graph the same idea appears as a straight line that passes through the origin, and a straight line that misses the origin is linear without being proportional.

questions.explanation: The defining feature of proportionality is a fixed ratio rather than a fixed difference, and the two can look alike in a table while behaving differently as the numbers grow. Division is the operation that exposes the ratio, and a single row with a drifting ratio settles the question against proportionality. A joining fee is the usual culprit in practice, because it shifts every output by the same amount and so changes the ratio without changing the shape of the graph.
questions.hint: Divide output by input in every row and see whether the answer repeats.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain why a linear model should not be pushed far past the data
questions.stem: Explain why a linear rule fitted to a short record should not be used far beyond the data that produced it, and name the assumption that each further step makes.

answer.exemplar: A linear rule fitted to a record says that the quantity changes by one constant amount for each unit of the input, and the fit only establishes that over the range where it was measured. Each step beyond that range asks the same question of a part of the rule nobody checked, so the further the input moves from the data, the more of the answer is supplied by the assumption rather than by evidence. The failure is often visible in the sign: a rule for seats needed, or for hours of work available, will eventually report a negative quantity, and a negative count is not a plausible prediction but a signal that the model has been used outside the range it describes. Sensible practice is to state the interval over which the model was checked, to mark values outside it as extrapolations rather than measurements, and to report the constant step itself as an assumption that could change. A model does not fail at a particular input because the arithmetic is wrong there; it fails because the question being asked has moved away from the situation the rule was built for.

questions.explanation: Every input a linear rule accepts is a claim that the same constant step continues, and only some of those claims were ever supported by data, so the useful habit is to name the range rather than to trust the formula everywhere. Impossible outputs such as negative counts or impossible lengths are the cheapest and most reliable warning that the model is being applied outside its intended situation. Recording the interval of validity alongside the model costs one sentence and prevents a confident number from being quoted as though it had been measured.
questions.hint: Think about which part of the rule the data actually tested, and what the rest of the rule is assuming.
